title: 8. Stage 2 Technical Structure, Trend Damage & Entry Timing

web_blocks.html: The technical record is damaged in the short term and intact in the long term. On 12 November 2026 the stock closed at ₹2,468.40, down 4.4% over one week and 16.8% over one month. It sits 21% below its 52-week high of ₹3,127.90, although it remains well above its 52-week low of ₹1,360.00. The figures in this chapter come from the same-session market ledger as of the 12 November close. The TradingView readings from the 13 November intraday feed are shown separately and are labelled as such, because that session was not complete when the report was assembled. The extension rows in the momentum table and the 50-day average of ₹2,706.93 in the stage evidence come from that intraday feed; on the 12 November close and the ledger 50-day average of ₹2,721.59, the extension from the 50-day average is about −9.3% and from the 10-week EMA of ₹2,593.11 (13 November feed) about −4.8%.

The market-facts trend filter classifies AZAD as Stage 3, the topping and pullback phase. The company-specific stage evaluation reads the same stage and returns a WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT_RETEST posture with a technical timing gate of CAP_WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT. AZAD is not in the current TheWrap Stage 2 leaderboard, so no external list supports the name. The two systems agree, and neither one offers a buy signal. Stage 3 means the advance has stalled and distribution has begun; it is the stage a buyer should wait out, not the stage to enter.

web_blocks.takeaway: The long trend is alive, but the short and intermediate structure has broken, and the decline has come with persistent distribution.

web_blocks.html: Price sits below its 20-day and 50-day averages, and the 50-day average is itself falling. The 200-day average at ₹2,186.39 is still well below price, so the long trend has not broken. That combination is the signature of a pullback inside a larger advance: the medium-term structure has cracked while the long-term structure still holds. RSI at 40.2 shows weak momentum rather than the oversold extreme that usually marks a bottom, which is why we do not call the decline finished.

The nearest structural shelf is ₹2,385.10, where the 20-day swing low and the 63-day base low coincide. It sits only 3.4% below the close, so the first test could come quickly. The support zone of ₹2,175.84 to ₹2,242.10 lies below it and is the area where the timing gate would consider an entry. Its anchor is the 13 November intraday TradingView daily S1 pivot of ₹2,208.97, since the 12 November ledger has no pivot level. The stop at ₹2,151.41 sits below that zone. It uses the 13 November feed’s ATR of ₹115.12; on the 12 November ledger’s ATR of ₹119.03 it would sit at about ₹2,149. On that stop the top-of-zone asymmetry is about 1.41 to 1, and the REJECTED verdict does not change. A break of ₹2,385 is the first warning, and a daily close below ₹2,151.41 cancels the setup entirely.

The 13 November intraday feed shows a 4-hour RSI of 44.2 against a daily RSI of 41.8, and the engine flags no 4-hour turn. A turn would require a higher low above the ₹2,385 shelf, a reclaim of the 20-day average and then a sustained close above it. One positive session does not meet that bar, so we do not infer a reversal from it.

Volume is quiet rather than decisive. The latest session traded at 0.7 times its 20-day average, which is not the surge that accompanies a turning point. Seven distribution days in the last 25 sessions tell the opposite story of the decline: heavier selling than buying on the down days. Relative strength of −28.5% over 28 sessions and −3.5% over 63 sessions confirms that the stock has fallen well behind its benchmark in the last month. Volume alone cannot tell us whether the selling is finished.

The timing judgment is therefore patient. The chart does not reject the stock on its own, because the long trend is intact. It does refuse a purchase today: the price sits 3.8% below the 20-day average and 9.3% below the falling 50-day average. A stabilisation between ₹2,175.84 and ₹2,242.10 that holds without a daily close below ₹2,151.41, followed by a reclaim of the 20-day average at ₹2,566.78, would move the timing gate. Even then the valuation check in Chapter 9 has to clear separately.

The options overlay is short. AZAD has no NSE F&O chain in the snapshot, so the options status is NOT_OPTIONABLE_OR_ILLIQUID. Any position would be cash equity with full downside exposure. The options snapshot also carries an embedded business-quality label of COMPOUNDER_PASS, which conflicts with the CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL verdict from the price-blind first pass. This dossier uses the first-pass verdict and flags the conflict rather than let a stale label drive the call.

The arithmetic that matters is simple. Entering at the top of the support zone, ₹2,242.10, against the stop at ₹2,151.41 risks ₹90.69 a share. The base-case value of ₹2,373 offers ₹130.90 of reward, which is 1.44 to 1. That is below our 1.5 to 1 minimum for any non-rejected call. The chart therefore earns a monitor role, not a purchase. Chapter 9 explains why the new-capital verdict is REJECTED on this basis rather than WAIT_FOR_SUPPORT.

Revisit the timing call only if the stock tests and holds the ₹2,175.84 to ₹2,242.10 zone without a daily close below ₹2,151.41, then closes back above the ₹2,566.78 20-day average. The valuation asymmetry still has to reach 1.5 to 1 before any purchase is considered.

book_paragraphs: Let us read the chart before we read the price target, because the chart tells us whether anyone is willing to buy today. On 12 November the stock closed at ₹2,468.40. That is down 4.4% in a week and 16.8% in a month, and about 21% below the 52-week high. Over one year the share is still well up. That is exactly why this setup is dangerous: a stock that has risen sharply can fall a long way from its high before the long trend gives way.

The trend filter puts AZAD in Stage 3, the topping and pullback phase. Stage 2 is the advancing phase we want to buy into, and Stage 3 is where the advance stalls and selling starts to accumulate. The company’s own stage evaluation reads the same stage and asks for a retest of support before any entry. AZAD is not on the current TheWrap Stage 2 leaderboard either, so no external list is holding the name up. Both systems agree, and neither one offers a buy signal.

Now look at the averages. The close sits below the 20-day average of ₹2,566.78 and the 50-day average of ₹2,721.59, and the 50-day average is falling. It sits above the 200-day average of ₹2,186.39, so the long trend has not broken. RSI at 40.2 is weak but not oversold. That is what a pullback looks like inside a larger advance, and it is why we are careful about calling the bottom. A bottom usually arrives with a much more violent reading than this.

Where would support have to appear? The nearest shelf is ₹2,385.10, the 20-day swing low and the 63-day base low, only 3.4% below the close. The support zone of ₹2,175.84 to ₹2,242.10 sits below it, anchored by the 13 November intraday S1 pivot near ₹2,209. The stop at ₹2,151.41 sits below that zone. It uses the 13 November feed’s ATR of ₹115.12; on the 12 November ledger’s ATR of ₹119.03 it would sit at about ₹2,149. On that stop the top-of-zone asymmetry is about 1.41 to 1, and the REJECTED verdict does not change. If the stock breaks ₹2,385, that is a warning. If a daily close falls below ₹2,151.41, the setup is cancelled and we stop thinking about the name as a chart trade.

The intraday picture from 13 November does not change the call. A 4-hour RSI of 44 against a daily RSI of 42 is a slight improvement, and the engine still flags no 4-hour turn. A real turn would need a higher low above ₹2,385, a reclaim of the 20-day average and a sustained close above it. One good session is not enough. The data here is intraday and incomplete, so we use it to confirm the picture, not to set a price.

Volume is the tempting signal, and it is the weakest one here. The latest session traded at 0.7 times its 20-day average, which is quiet. Seven distribution days in the last 25 sessions show heavier selling than buying on the down days. Relative strength of minus 28.5% over 28 sessions says the stock has lagged its benchmark badly. Those three facts together describe a stock still being sold, not one that has finished being sold.

The options overlay is simple. AZAD has no NSE F&O chain in the snapshot, so there is no liquid options structure to analyse. Any exposure would be cash equity with the full downside. The options snapshot also carries a business label of COMPOUNDER_PASS, which contradicts our first-pass verdict of CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL. We keep the first-pass verdict and disclose the conflict, because a stale label should never override the evidence we gathered without seeing the price.

The arithmetic is where patience pays. Enter at the top of the support zone, ₹2,242.10, and the stop at ₹2,151.41 risks about ₹91 a share. The base value of ₹2,373 offers about ₹131 of reward. That is 1.44 to 1, short of our minimum of 1.5 to 1. The chart is not what rules the stock out. The chart simply tells us the price has not yet reached a level where the reward is large enough, and the valuation chapter says the gap is not closing quickly enough.

Here is how you and I would use the chart. First, mark the ₹2,385 shelf and the ₹2,176 to ₹2,242 zone. Then wait to see whether the stock holds that zone without a daily close below ₹2,151. Next, look for a higher low and a reclaim of the 20-day average at ₹2,567. Only after that would the timing gate open. A single bounce from the zone is not a hold, and a single intraday recovery is not a trend.

The No-FOMO sizing table in Chapter 9 shows what a position would look like if the verdict were different. It is a ceiling and a mechanical illustration, not an allocation. It turns the stop distance into a risk unit, and it assumes you can buy at the price the stop allows. If price gaps through ₹2,151, the modelled loss is a floor rather than a guarantee, because a stop can fill lower. Limit discipline and accepting missed trades are worth more than the number of shares you could buy.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A chart can tell you whether buyers are present. It cannot tell you whether the business earns enough to justify the price they are paying. Keep those two questions apart and answer the timing question first, because it is the one that changes every day. The valuation question changes slowly, and it is the one that decides whether the timing question matters at all.
